## NGO Website Development in India: Handling Offline Donations — Bank Transfer, Cheque, Cash and QR Pledges — on a Donation Website Without Losing Track of Receipts

An NGO website can accept offline donations safely by treating them as pledges first and receipts second: the donor fills in a short pledge form, the site shows the bank details or a QR code with a unique reference, the donor pays outside the website, and your team matches the money to the pledge in the admin panel before issuing a receipt. This keeps every rupee linked to a named donor, a purpose and a record, which is what 80G receipts, audits and donor trust all depend on. If you are planning NGO website development in India and assume that "donation" means only card and UPI payments at checkout, you will miss a large part of how Indian supporters actually give.

Many donors still prefer to transfer from their own bank, send a cheque, hand over cash at an event or pay through a company's payroll or CSR process. Major donors and trusts often insist on bank transfer. Local supporters may walk into the office. If the website has no way to capture these gifts, they end up in a notebook, a WhatsApp chat or a spreadsheet kept by one volunteer, and months later nobody can tell who gave what. This guide explains how to design the offline-donation flow on your website: the pledge form, the bank details page, reference codes, how cheques and cash are logged, how reconciliation works, what to say to donors, and where compliance questions (80G, PAN, foreign contributions) require advice from your own accountant or legal adviser. We avoid quoting figures we cannot source; wherever a rule depends on the current statute, we mark it for you to confirm.

## Why offline donations deserve a proper flow

Online checkout produces a tidy record automatically: a transaction ID, an amount, a donor and a timestamp. Offline giving does not, which is why it is where records go wrong. Typical problems are:

- A bank statement shows "NEFT from R K Sharma ₹25,000", and no one knows which campaign or which person it relates to.
- A donor says they transferred last week; your team cannot find it because the statement shows a company account name.
- A cheque is deposited but the donor's PAN and address were never collected, so the receipt cannot be issued.
- Cash received at an event is entered in a register with no link to a donor record.
- The same donor appears under three spellings, so their giving history, and their eligibility for a combined annual statement, is fragmented.

A well-designed flow solves these by capturing the donor's details before the money moves, giving every pledge a reference, and giving staff a single screen for matching. It also supports the donor: they receive a clear confirmation, know exactly where to send the money and get a receipt without chasing.

## The core idea: pledge, pay, match, receipt

The flow has four stages. Everything else in this article is detail on one of them.

1. **Pledge.** The donor tells the NGO what they intend to give: name, contact, amount, purpose, payment method (bank transfer, cheque, cash drop-off, QR), PAN if needed and address for the receipt.
2. **Pay.** The website shows how to pay for the chosen method and gives a unique pledge reference. The donor pays outside the site.
3. **Match.** Staff match incoming bank entries, cheques or cash receipts to pledges and mark them as received, partially received or not received.
4. **Receipt.** On confirmed receipt, the system issues the acknowledgement or 80G receipt, updates the donor's history and closes the pledge.

Notice that the website never claims money has arrived until staff confirm it. That distinction between "pledged" and "received" is the most important design principle in the whole flow, and it should be visible in the data model, the admin screens and the emails.

## The pledge form

Keep the form short but complete enough to produce a receipt. Collect only what you need, in keeping with the principle of data minimisation under India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act; our guide to [donor data protection under the DPDP Act](/blog/ngo-donor-data-protection-dpdp-act-2026) explains what notice and consent your form should include.

### Fields to include

- **Donor type:** individual, company, trust or other organisation. The fields differ for each.
- **Full name** as it should appear on the receipt, and for organisations, the registered name and contact person.
- **Email and mobile number,** so you can confirm and follow up.
- **Amount and currency,** with a note if you accept only Indian rupees.
- **Purpose or campaign:** general fund, a named project, corpus, or sponsorship. Offering a dropdown reduces ambiguity.
- **Payment method:** bank transfer (NEFT, RTGS, IMPS), cheque or demand draft, cash at office or event, or a QR/UPI payment made later.
- **PAN,** where your receipt process requires it. Explain why you ask. Ask your accountant which cases need PAN under current rules rather than collecting it from everyone by default.
- **Address for the receipt,** including PIN code.
- **Citizenship or residency status,** if you accept foreign contributions, because those are governed by separate rules (see the FCRA section below).
- **Consent checkboxes** for processing data and, separately and optionally, for updates by email or WhatsApp.
- **Expected date of payment,** which helps staff match entries.

### Fields to leave out

Do not ask for bank account passwords, card numbers or OTPs. An offline-pledge form should never collect payment credentials. Do not ask for more personal data than needed to issue a receipt. If you add a free-text message field, make clear that donors should not enter sensitive information.

### Confirmation page and email

After submission, show a confirmation page and send an email containing:

- the pledge reference code;
- the amount and purpose;
- clear payment instructions for the chosen method;
- a note on what the donor should send you after paying (for example, the transaction reference or a screenshot, if you choose to request one);
- the expected timeline for the receipt;
- a contact for questions.

State plainly that the pledge is not a receipt. If your website sends a "thank you" with the word "receipt" before money has arrived, donors may treat it as proof of payment.

## The bank-details page

A page with your bank details should be easy to find, accurate and hard to tamper with.

- **Show the legal account name, bank, branch, account number and IFSC code** that your accountant confirms. Keep the account type that receives donations separate from operational accounts where your auditors require that.
- **Offer a copy button** for each field; copying reduces typing mistakes.
- **Explain the reference.** Ask donors to put the pledge reference in the transfer remarks or narration field, and explain that not every bank keeps long remarks, so a short code works best.
- **Protect the page.** Fraudsters sometimes copy NGO sites and change account numbers. Use HTTPS, restrict who can edit the bank details in the CMS (see our guide to [CMS roles and staff updates](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-cms-roles-staff-updates-2026)), log every change, and require a second person to approve it. Add a visible "last reviewed" date.
- **Publish the same details everywhere,** including printed material, and make sure they match. A mismatch between a brochure and the website is itself a warning sign to careful donors.
- **Do not hide the page in an image.** Text can be read by screen readers and copied; accessibility affects donor trust, as discussed in our article on [accessibility and donor trust](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-accessibility-donor-trust-2026).

### Different accounts for different donors

If you accept foreign contributions, you will have a designated account for them, and domestic donations belong in a different one. The website must show the right account to the right donor, and must not mix them. Get this wrong and you create a compliance problem. See the FCRA note below.

## QR codes and UPI for offline-style giving

A UPI QR code printed on a poster, a standee or a letter is "offline" in the sense that the donor pays outside the website, but it is still instant and traceable by the bank. Two design points matter.

- **Use unique references wherever possible.** A single static QR code will give you payments with no reference to a pledge. If you can, generate a pledge-specific payment link or QR code, or ask donors to enter the pledge reference in the UPI note.
- **Reconcile against bank statements,** not just app notifications. Our article on [UPI donation reconciliation](/blog/upi-donation-reconciliation-ngo-workflow) describes the admin fields and exports a reconciliation process needs.

Be mindful of fee and policy changes in UPI that may affect your costs; see our post on [NPCI UPI MDR rules for donation checkouts](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-upi-mdr-2026).

## Cheques and demand drafts

Cheques are slower and create more steps, so the admin side matters.

- **Record the cheque details at pledge or receipt:** cheque number, date, bank, amount and payer name.
- **Track statuses:** promised, received at office, deposited, cleared, bounced. A cheque that bounces must reverse the receipt or prevent it being issued.
- **Do not issue the receipt until clearance** unless your policy and your accountant allow otherwise. A clear internal rule avoids arguments later.
- **Handle post-dated cheques carefully;** record the date and set a reminder.
- **Allow donors to upload a photograph** of the cheque only if you have a secure process for storing it. Cheque images contain account numbers, so store them with restricted access, or avoid collecting them.

## Cash donations

Cash needs the most care, for both compliance and security.

- **Know the rules.** Indian tax law places conditions on cash donations: for example, deductions under the 80G scheme have historically not been available for cash donations above a stated threshold, and there are limits on cash receipts more generally. Because the Income-tax Act was replaced from 1 April 2026 and section numbers changed, do not quote section numbers or thresholds on the website without confirming them with your chartered accountant. TODO: confirm the current cash-donation limit and wording under the new Act before publishing any figure.
- **Issue receipts at the point of collection** from a numbered receipt book or a mobile receipt app linked to the donor database, and enter each one into the system the same day.
- **Never record cash only in a notebook.** Use a short admin form: date, collector, donor, amount, purpose, receipt number and event or location.
- **Two-person handling** for cash at events and a deposit routine with a bank slip attached to the record.
- **Discourage large cash gifts** on the website by pointing donors to bank transfer; say why in a sentence (traceability and receipts).

## Matching incoming money to pledges: the reconciliation screen

The admin panel needs one screen where staff match reality to pledges. Specify it clearly to your developer.

### What it should show

- A list of open pledges with reference, donor, amount, method, expected date and age.
- An import or entry area for bank statement lines (CSV from the bank, or manual entry): date, amount, narration, bank reference.
- Suggested matches based on amount, reference code in the narration and donor name.
- Actions: match, mark partially received, mark as unmatched, reject, or merge duplicate pledges.
- Unmatched incoming amounts that do not correspond to any pledge, so staff can contact the sender and create a record.

### Statuses to model

| Status | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Pledged | Donor submitted the form; no money confirmed |
| Awaiting payment | Reminder sent; past expected date |
| Partially received | Some amount has been matched |
| Received | Full amount matched and verified |
| Receipt issued | Acknowledgement or 80G receipt sent |
| Cancelled or lapsed | Donor withdrew or no money arrived after a set period |
| Bounced or reversed | Cheque or transfer failed after being recorded |

### Reminders and lapse rules

Send a polite reminder a few days after the expected date, then another, and set a point (for example 30 days, a number you decide) after which an open pledge is marked lapsed after a final message. Do not pressure donors; a gentle, factual reminder is enough. Count lapsed pledges as a metric rather than deleting them.

### Audit trail

Every status change should store who made it and when. When auditors ask how a particular ₹50,000 entry was received and receipted, the log answers. Keep the matching evidence (bank line, cheque number, cash receipt number) attached to the donor record.

## Receipts, 80G and annual statements

Once a pledge is marked received, the receipt flow should follow the same rules as an online donation.

- **Receipt content and numbering** must follow what your accountant specifies for 80G and for your trust or society's own records; for the website's side of this, see [80G-compliant donation platforms](/blog/80g-compliant-donation-platform-india) and our note on [automated 80G receipts and common errors](/blog/automated-80g-receipts-ngo-errors).
- **Use the date of actual receipt** of money, not the date of the pledge, wherever your accountant says that is the relevant date.
- **Issue one receipt per confirmed payment,** and avoid editing receipts after issue; cancel and reissue with a note if a correction is needed.
- **Combine offline and online giving in the donor's history,** so that a supporter who gave online in April and by bank transfer in October sees both in one place. This is where a donor account area helps; see [donor account areas with giving history and receipts](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-donor-account-giving-history-receipts-2026).
- **Annual reporting.** Donor-wise statements and any annual reporting your 80G approval requires depend on clean records; if you need a refresher, read our [12A and 80G renewal checklist](/blog/12a-80g-renewal-checklist-ngos).

## Foreign contributions and FCRA

If your NGO is registered under the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act, foreign contributions must go through the designated account and are subject to separate record-keeping and reporting. The website's job is to avoid mixing streams.

- **Ask for residency or citizenship status** on the pledge form where you accept international gifts, and route the donor to the correct instructions.
- **Show FCRA account details only to the donors it applies to,** in line with your compliance adviser's guidance.
- **Do not accept foreign money into a domestic account** or the reverse. If a payment lands in the wrong account, record it and consult your adviser immediately.

If your organisation is not FCRA-registered, say so clearly on the page and do not accept contributions from foreign sources. For related compliance topics see our posts on [FCRA amendment rules](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-fcra-amendment-rules-2026) and on [setting up a payment gateway under FCRA](/blog/fcra-payment-gateway-setup-ngos).

## Corporate, CSR and trust donors

Institutional donors behave differently and often require specific documents.

- **Provide a "donate as an organisation" path** that collects registered name, PAN, GSTIN if relevant, authorised signatory and contact.
- **Offer a downloadable details sheet** with the NGO's registration numbers, bank details, and the relevant approvals, but only with information your trustees agree to publish.
- **Support a purchase order or invoice-style request** if a company requires one before paying.
- **Explain your CSR eligibility accurately.** Whether a company's gift counts as CSR spending depends on registrations and the nature of the project; do not claim eligibility you have not verified. For the context, see our article on [CSR and the Social Stock Exchange](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-csr-social-stock-exchange-2026) and on [CSR volunteer portals](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-csr-volunteer-portals-2026).

## Security, fraud and privacy considerations

- **Restrict admin access** to the pledge and bank data; only finance staff should see PAN and bank references.
- **Protect against fake pledges.** Add spam protection to the form (see [contact-form spam and bot protection](/blog/website-designer-pune-contact-form-spam-bot-protection-2026)) and rate-limit submissions.
- **Warn donors about impersonation.** A one-line notice such as "We will never ask you to pay to a personal account or UPI ID" helps.
- **Encrypt and limit retention** of personal data; delete or anonymise data you no longer need, following your privacy notice.
- **Back up the pledge database** and test restores; see [website backups and disaster recovery](/blog/web-development-company-pune-website-backups-disaster-recovery-2026).
- **Keep the page performant on mobile.** Many donors open the details page on a low-bandwidth phone, as we discuss in [designing for low-bandwidth mobile donors](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-low-bandwidth-mobile-donors-2026).

## How to brief your developer

Give your developer a one-page specification, including:

1. The donor types and the pledge form fields, with which are mandatory.
2. The payment methods and the instruction text for each.
3. The reference-code format (short, easy to type, not guessable; for example a prefix plus a number).
4. The statuses and transitions in the table above.
5. The admin screen for matching, including bank-statement CSV import.
6. The receipt rules and who approves them.
7. The email templates for pledge confirmation, reminder, receipt and lapse.
8. Role permissions: who can create, match, edit and approve.
9. The audit trail and export requirements for auditors.
10. The test cases: a bank transfer, a cheque that clears, a cheque that bounces, a cash gift at an event, a partial payment, a duplicate pledge and an overseas donor.

If you use a donor management system or CRM, decide where pledges live. Keeping a single donor record across online and offline channels is a major reason to connect the website to a donor CRM; see our overview of [donor CRM software for Indian NGOs](/blog/ngo-donor-crm-software-india-2026). Our [NGO website development](/pages/ngopage) work covers donation flows, receipts and admin panels of this kind, and our [website creation](/services/website-creation) team can scope the pledge module for an existing site.


Related reading: Donors who give by cheque or transfer in memory of someone need the same dedication details captured; see our guide to [tribute and in-memory donations](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-tribute-in-memory-gift-donations-dedication-forms-2026).

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Can an NGO website accept donations by bank transfer?

Yes. The usual method is a pledge form that records the donor's details and gives a reference code, followed by a page showing the bank details. Staff then match the bank entry to the pledge and issue a receipt once the money is confirmed.

### How do we link a bank transfer to the right donor?

Ask donors to put the pledge reference in the transfer remarks, and match entries in the admin panel using amount, reference and donor name. Keep a screen for unmatched amounts so that staff can contact senders whose transfers carry no reference.

### Should we issue a receipt when a cheque is received or when it clears?

Many organisations wait until the cheque clears, because a bounced cheque would otherwise need a reversal. Confirm your own policy with your accountant and apply it consistently, recording both the received and cleared dates.

### Can an NGO accept cash donations through its website?

A website cannot collect cash, but it can record cash gifts received at an office or event with a numbered receipt and a linked donor record. Tax rules limit cash donations in several ways, so confirm current limits with your chartered accountant before you publish any figure.

### How do we keep offline and online donors in one record?

Use a single donor database, with pledges, online payments and offline receipts all linked to the same donor profile. Match on email, mobile number and PAN where lawfully collected, and merge duplicates through an admin action that keeps an audit trail.

## Sources and notes

Rules on 80G, cash donations, PAN and receipts, and on foreign contributions, change with the law and with government notices; confirm them with your chartered accountant or legal adviser before you publish any figure on your site.
